newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea seeks to allay fears on OECD entry.
newsitem.headline: South Korea seeks to allay fears on OECD entry.

text.p: South Korea attempted on Thursday to allay fears the country was not ready to join the Paris-based OECD club of industrialised nations, predicting parliament would ratify membership by mid-December.

Finance ministry officials told foreign journalists the South Korean economy had all the necessary ingredients to continue strong growth with a mix of low inflation, stable financial markets and increasing productivity.

South Korea, invited last Friday to become Asia's second member of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, was targeting annual inflation of 2-3 percent by the year 2000, in line with other OECD members, they said.

"We're continuing to put a lot of effort into reducing inflation," said Cho Yoon-je, senior counsellor to the Finance Minister, adding that he expected inflation to run at 4.5-5.0 percent for 1996, nearly unchanged from 1995.

Those levels are far less worrisome than the eight-to-nine percent inflation of the early 1990s, and Cho stressed South Korean price stability would soon come to mirror that of its more industrialised international peers.
But opposition parties are threatening to block entry into the OECD club by opposing ratification in parliament, where President Kim Young-sam's ruling party has a slim majority.

The opposition parties warn of the destabilising effects of prying open local markets to offshore competition any faster, especially on small and medium-sized industries, and say OECD membership could entail painful structural changes.

They also fear entry into the OECD will hamper the economy by triggering a rush of speculative funds, or "hot money", into local markets as investors focus on South Korea's relatively high interest rates, now hovering around 12 percent.
The Citizens Coalition for Economic Justice, one of South Korea's major lobby groups, has said it would mount a nationwide campaign to block ratification of OECD admission.
But Cho said South Korea would ensure stability by adhering to a strict timetable for opening markets and dismissed criticism that Seoul was inviting a financial crisis.
"The opposition does not have a concrete case," he said.
"We should get it (OECD membership) passed by the end of the current session," he said. The current session of the National Assembly is scheduled to end on December 18.
Spending on foreign aid would increase if South Korea joined the OECD, said Kang Suk-in, deputy director general of international policy at the finance ministry.
He said foreign aid spending would rise from a current 0.05 percent of gross national product to the OECD average of 0.3 percent, albeit at a gradual pace.
South Korea would be the OECD's 11th largest exporter, accounting for about 2.5 percent of world exports, a position which had been enhanced through liberalisation of import controls.
Since the early 1990s, South Korea has taken steps to open its markets slowly, offering to announce new measures to speed up the process if it won OECD membership.

On October 1, the ceiling on foreign ownership in local stocks was raised to 20 percent for most South Korean listed companies from 18 percent. The government has pledged to expand the ceiling by three percentage points every year by 1999.
Foreign investment in unsecured corporate bonds issued by small and medium-sized firms will be allowed from late 1998.
